segments.chapter_title: Hook
segments.text: In its last financial year, Costco sold two hundred and ninety-seven billion dollars' worth of stuff. Groceries, TVs, tires, gasoline, and a very large number of rotisserie chickens.

segments.chapter_title: Hook
segments.text: After paying for all those goods, and for every warehouse, every worker and every truck, about five point eight billion dollars were left from those sales. Less than two cents on the dollar.

segments.chapter_title: Hook
segments.text: Then there's a second line in the accounts. Five point nine billion dollars, from eighty-four million people paying for a plastic card.

segments.chapter_title: Hook
segments.text: Those fees are about two percent of Costco's revenue. And about half of its operating profit.

segments.chapter_title: Hook
segments.text: So here's the claim we're going to test. Costco isn't really a store that charges a fee. It's a membership that comes with a store attached.

segments.chapter_title: Hook
segments.text: Let's take the receipt apart, line by line.

segments.chapter_title: Where $100 at Costco really goes
segments.text: Costco's financial year ended on August thirtieth, 2026. Total revenue: three hundred and three billion dollars. Almost all of it is what Costco calls net sales, the goods. The rest, five point nine billion, is membership fees.

segments.chapter_title: Where $100 at Costco really goes
segments.text: Now follow one hundred dollars spent at the checkout.

segments.chapter_title: Where $100 at Costco really goes
segments.text: About eighty-nine dollars go straight back to the companies that made the goods. That's what Costco paid for the merchandise.

segments.chapter_title: Where $100 at Costco really goes
segments.text: Another nine dollars and fifteen cents pay for running everything else: wages, warehouses, electricity, card fees, head office.

segments.chapter_title: Where $100 at Costco really goes
segments.text: What's left from the sale itself: one dollar and ninety-four cents.

segments.chapter_title: Where $100 at Costco really goes
segments.text: Now add the membership. For every hundred dollars of sales, members also pay Costco about two dollars in fees. And unlike a sale, a fee doesn't come with any goods to pay for.

segments.chapter_title: Where $100 at Costco really goes
segments.text: Put the two together, and Costco makes about three dollars and ninety-three cents of operating profit on every hundred dollars of sales. After interest and taxes, it keeps about three dollars and ten cents.

segments.chapter_title: Where $100 at Costco really goes
segments.text: Over the whole year, that's eleven point seven billion dollars of operating profit. Roughly half came from what's on the shelves. The other half came from the card.

segments.chapter_title: Where $100 at Costco really goes
segments.text: For comparison, American food retailers keep about two cents of net profit per dollar, according to their industry group. So Costco isn't poor. It just makes its money in a strange place.

segments.chapter_title: Where $100 at Costco really goes
segments.text: Which raises the question: why would a store choose to make so little on the things it sells?

segments.chapter_title: The shelves: priced to barely break even
segments.text: On everything it sells, Costco's gross margin was eleven point oh nine percent last year. That's the slice left after paying suppliers, before any other cost. Costco's own annual report says its volume lets it operate profitably at "significantly lower gross margins" than most retailers.

segments.chapter_title: The shelves: priced to barely break even
segments.text: That's not an accident. For decades, Costco has been reported to cap its markups: around fourteen percent on national brands, and fifteen percent on its own brand. It's not written in the annual report. But the eleven percent is.

segments.chapter_title: The shelves: priced to barely break even
segments.text: That own brand is Kirkland Signature. Costco's finance chief says Kirkland products are priced at least fifteen to twenty percent below the national brand equivalent. Store brands made up just under a third of Costco's sales in late 2024.

segments.chapter_title: The shelves: priced to barely break even
segments.text: And when Costco's own costs fall, it tends to pass the saving on. On its latest earnings call, it listed price cuts: Kirkland walnuts from thirteen seventy-nine to nine ninety-nine. Black pepper from six ninety-nine to five ninety-nine.

segments.chapter_title: The shelves: priced to barely break even
segments.text: Then there's the most famous price in retail. A hot dog and a soda for one dollar and fifty cents. Same price since 1985. If it had followed inflation, it would cost about four sixty-five today.

segments.chapter_title: The shelves: priced to barely break even
segments.text: In March 2026, Costco's chief executive, Ron Vachris, was asked about it. His answer: "The hot dog price will not change as long as I'm around."

segments.chapter_title: The shelves: priced to barely break even
segments.text: Why would a company with three hundred billion dollars of sales care about a hot dog? Because at Costco, a price isn't only a way to make money on an item. It's an advertisement for the card. Every member who sees a one-fifty hot dog, or a cheaper bag of walnuts, gets one more reason to renew.

segments.chapter_title: The shelves: priced to barely break even
segments.text: A normal retailer that finds a cheaper supplier keeps the difference as profit. Costco mostly passes it on. In its finance chief's words: "Our goal is to be the first to lower prices where we see opportunities to do so." A member who feels the savings is worth more than a few extra cents on one item.

segments.chapter_title: The shelves: priced to barely break even
segments.text: But selling at eleven percent margins only works if you can also run a store for less than anyone else.

segments.chapter_title: How to run a store on eleven cents
segments.text: Here's the first trick. Choice.

segments.chapter_title: How to run a store on eleven cents
segments.text: An average American supermarket carries about thirty-three thousand different items. A Costco warehouse is more than three times bigger, and carries fewer than four thousand.

segments.chapter_title: How to run a store on eleven cents
segments.text: Think one or two brands of ketchup, not twenty. In a giant pack. On a pallet.

segments.chapter_title: How to run a store on eleven cents
segments.text: That does a lot of work. With so few items, each one sells in enormous volume. Costco's annual report says it plainly: those volumes, and how fast the goods turn over, are what let it live on such thin margins. Fewer items also means bigger orders for each supplier, and fewer, bigger things to unload and stock.

segments.chapter_title: How to run a store on eleven cents
segments.text: The result is a staggering amount of sales per building. Costco runs nine hundred and thirty-nine warehouses. Divide its sales by that, and each one does more than three hundred million dollars a year. Its closest rival, Walmart's Sam's Club, runs six hundred and one clubs, with ninety-three billion dollars of sales. That's about one hundred and fifty-five million each. Roughly half.

segments.chapter_title: How to run a store on eleven cents
segments.text: Here's the part that surprises people. Costco isn't cheap because it pays people badly.

segments.chapter_title: How to run a store on eleven cents
segments.text: It has about three hundred and fifty-five thousand employees. In the US, the average hourly wage is around thirty-three dollars. In early 2025, it set its lowest starting rate at twenty dollars an hour.

segments.chapter_title: How to run a store on eleven cents
segments.text: And yet all its running costs, wages included, come to just nine point one five percent of sales. Not because each worker is cheap, but because each worker moves so much merchandise.

segments.chapter_title: How to run a store on eleven cents
segments.text: So the shelves make a little money, in a very efficient way. Now for the line that makes the rest.

segments.chapter_title: The card: what members are really buying
segments.text: At the end of August 2026, Costco had eighty-four point one million paid members. With the extra household cards, that's one hundred and fifty million people carrying one.

segments.chapter_title: The card: what members are really buying
segments.text: In the US, a basic membership costs sixty-five dollars a year. About half of paid members pay double that for the Executive card, one hundred and thirty dollars, which gives back two percent on most purchases, up to twelve hundred and fifty dollars a year.

segments.chapter_title: The card: what members are really buying
segments.text: Now the number that matters most. In the US and Canada, ninety-two point three percent of members renew.

segments.chapter_title: The card: what members are really buying
segments.text: Think about what that means. Almost every year, more than nine in ten customers pay again, up front, before they've bought anything. Costco can count that money in advance, and it spreads it evenly over the year in its accounts.

segments.chapter_title: The card: what members are really buying
segments.text: Costco says it openly. In its latest earnings call, Ron Vachris called membership "the most important item we sell".

segments.chapter_title: The card: what members are really buying
segments.text: And like any product, it can get a price increase. In September 2024, Costco raised its fees for the first time since 2017: sixty to sixty-five dollars for the basic card, one hundred and twenty to one hundred and thirty for Executive.

segments.chapter_title: The card: what members are really buying
segments.text: Over the past year, membership income grew eleven percent. And renewal didn't fall. It ticked up.

segments.chapter_title: The card: what members are really buying
segments.text: The benefit from that increase is now fully in the numbers. In the last quarter, leaving aside the increase and currency effects, fee income still grew almost seven percent, simply because there are more members, and more of them on the expensive card.

segments.chapter_title: The card: what members are really buying
segments.text: And the members are getting younger. According to Ron Vachris, the number of members under forty has grown nearly sixty percent since the pandemic. They're now more than a quarter of the base. A thirty-year-old who renews today could keep paying for decades.

segments.chapter_title: The card: what members are really buying
segments.text: Here's the deal, then, in one sentence. Members pay Costco for the right to buy things at almost cost. And Costco has to keep those prices low, every single day, or that ninety-two percent starts to slip.

segments.chapter_title: The card: what members are really buying
segments.text: That's the real discipline behind the hot dog. Raise prices on the shelves, and you put the membership at risk. And the membership is where half the profit is.

segments.chapter_title: Gas, the app and the rivals
segments.text: Two parts of Costco are growing faster than the rest, and both serve the card.

segments.chapter_title: Gas, the app and the rivals
segments.text: First, gasoline. Costco ran seven hundred and seventy-four gas stations at the end of its year, and fuel made up eleven percent of its sales. When prices at the pump jumped in 2026, drivers came in droves: in the last quarter, gas sales were up by more than thirty percent.

segments.chapter_title: Gas, the app and the rivals
segments.text: Costco doesn't say how much it earns on fuel. But it says gas brings in new members, and that members who fill up there tend to spend more inside.

segments.chapter_title: Gas, the app and the rivals
segments.text: Second, online. Costco's digital sales passed thirty-three billion dollars last year, up more than twenty percent. Same model, just without the walk past the pallets.

segments.chapter_title: Gas, the app and the rivals
segments.text: And the machine is still running hot. In September 2026, Costco's sales were up thirteen percent. Without the effect of gas prices and currencies, comparable sales were up almost eight percent.

segments.chapter_title: Gas, the app and the rivals
segments.text: What about the competition? In its annual report, Costco lists Walmart, Target, Kroger and Amazon, plus the other warehouse clubs, Sam's Club and BJ's.

segments.chapter_title: Gas, the app and the rivals
segments.text: Several of them run the same playbook. Walmart says membership income is a significant part of Sam's Club's profit. And Amazon Prime is another way of charging shoppers up front, so that they come back.

segments.chapter_title: Gas, the app and the rivals
segments.text: Costco's answer is to keep building. It opened twenty-eight warehouses last year, and plans thirty-three more this year, including in Europe, Canada and Mexico. Every new building is a new pool of people who can buy a card.

segments.chapter_title: Gas, the app and the rivals
segments.text: So the real fight isn't over who sells the cheapest ketchup. It's over which membership people decide is worth paying for again next year.

segments.chapter_title: So, how does Costco make money?
segments.text: So, how does Costco make money?

segments.chapter_title: So, how does Costco make money?
segments.text: On the goods, barely. About two dollars on every hundred, after costs. On the card, a lot. Almost six billion dollars a year, for a product that doesn't need a shelf.

segments.chapter_title: So, how does Costco make money?
segments.text: That doesn't mean the shelves don't matter. Without the cheap walnuts, the pallets and the one-fifty hot dog, nobody would pay sixty-five dollars to walk in. The shelves are the proof. The card is the business.

segments.chapter_title: So, how does Costco make money?
segments.text: And the lesson goes beyond Costco. The cheapest thing in the building is often there for a reason. Sometimes the price on the shelf isn't how a company makes money. It's how it convinces you to pay somewhere else.
